blocks.text: Experience Study: Status at the Midpoint

For {{fact:f:E-2019-001.client}}. Prepared by David Sherman, Senior Analyst. The study is at its midpoint. This report sets out the work done so far and what remains, and it makes no recommendation on any assumption.
In Brief

The data work for terminations, retirements and mortality is finished. The status history reconciles to the census in every year of the study period, and the experience for each of the three has been tabulated against the current assumptions. No assumption has yet been recommended. The study is on schedule and within budget.

One piece of data is still outstanding. The salary increase analysis needs the pay history for the earliest years of the study period, which we requested in the data summary. That analysis cannot start until the history arrives, and it is the item most likely to affect the schedule.
Work Completed This Period

1. We reconciled the status history to the year-end census for every year of the study period. The last gap, a group of internal transfers that payroll had recorded as new hires, closed when Megan Dudley linked the old and new employee numbers your staff supplied.

2. We received dates of birth for all but a few of the retiree records that lacked them. As agreed at the working session, the remaining records are excluded from the mortality tabulation, and the data summary lists each one.
3. We issued the data summary. It records every change made to the files, the source of each change, and every record excluded.

4. Jeffrey Ochoa split the early-service termination results by year of hire. The higher rate of departure appears in each hiring year, not in one, so it does not look like the effect of a single unusual year.
5. Robert Lawrence reviewed the tabulations and the approach to credibility. Drafting of the recommendations can begin.
Observed Experience

The table compares the experience the plan recorded with what the current assumptions predicted. These are measurements. None of them is a recommendation, and none should be read as a decision to change a rate.

header: Credibility of the plan's own data
rows: Terminations
More departures than expected in the first years of service and fewer than expected after that. The pattern holds in each hiring year.
Adequate in the early service years; thinner at longer service
Retirements
Fewer than expected in the early retirement window; close to expected at older ages
Adequate at the ages where most retirements occur
Mortality
Fewer retiree deaths than the current table predicts
Limited; the number of deaths is small

blocks.text: What We Have Assumed

We have relied on the census, the status history and the benefit records as your staff provided them. We reviewed them for consistency and completeness, as ASOP No. 23 requires, but we have not audited them.

Three treatments in the tabulations are our choices, not facts in the data, and the report will state each of them. Transferred employees are carried as continuing service. Rehired employees re-enter the active group from the date of rehire. Retiree records without a date of birth are left out instead of being given an assumed age.
Budget

Time charged through the midpoint is consistent with the fee of {{fact:f:E-2019-001.fee}} set out in the engagement letter, and we do not expect the remaining work to exceed it. If the pay history needs a second request or substantial correction, the added work could affect that expectation. We will raise it with you before that work begins.
Work Remaining
1. The salary increase analysis, once the pay history for the earliest years arrives. David Sherman will lead it.

2. Draft recommended assumptions for termination, retirement and mortality. Jeffrey Ochoa will prepare them, with the basis for each and the weight given to the plan's own experience. The mortality recommendation will also address future improvement, measured against the MP-2018 scale the Society of Actuaries published last October.
3. A working session with your staff to go through the draft recommendations before the report is written.
4. The draft report, followed by the final report once your comments are addressed. Robert Lawrence will sign the final report.
